name: Rafael Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, forty-three, and I'm a junior electrician wiring houses and helping with shop repairs. I have a vocational certificate, but I still need the senior electrician to check my tests and explain the harder faults. I used to help maintain a hotel, and I like finally understanding some of the work I used to pass to a contractor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Anya sews costumes for a small theatre workshop, and our children are six and fifteen. We have a mortgage, two months of expenses saved, typical electrician's pay coming from my job and a few other electrical firms nearby. I use AI every day for practice questions and to turn my notes into short explanations, then check the answers with the course book or supervisor. My current work agreement comes up for renewal in six months, which is already on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll keep the parts that help me learn and let the grand claims go. I'd show a colleague how I turn course notes into practice questions, but I wouldn't say that makes either of us a qualified tester. A shortcut to a question isn't a shortcut around a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the next renewal even if AI does very little. Two months saved is useful, but the mortgage doesn't pause while I ask another local firm whether it needs a junior. I'm keen on the trade; I'm less keen on telling the children a work agreement is something you simply trust to continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised shifts now and through the first year, asking next month what the employer needs for renewal. I'd spend twenty minutes each evening checking AI practice answers against my notes, taking disagreements to the supervisor. Anya and I would put off buying a larger second-hand car until the agreement is renewed in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but full of ideas while I'm actually learning. I can be excited by a new tool and worried about the payslip on the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why postpone the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present car runs, even if squeezing the children's bags in is a nuisance. I'd rather keep the deposit money available until I know the wage continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about renewal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which paid tasks I need to perform safely, who decides and when I'll hear. I want a date and a clear standard, not just a pat on the shoulder while someone walks away.

say: I'd keep **useful learning tools** even if the largest AI promises fade.
I think **practice questions** help us learn, but do not qualify a junior to skip safety checks.
think: I'm already **anxious about renewal**, even when AI adds little change to work.
Our **two-month cushion** cannot pause the mortgage while I search among the few nearby employers.
do: Keep **supervised shifts** and ask next month about written standards and dates for renewal.
Check **daily AI practice** against course notes and take disagreements to the supervisor.
Postpone the **larger used car** until the work agreement is renewed in writing.
feel: **Anxious but curious**, excited by learning while worrying about continued pay.
S0.quote: I can be excited by a new tool and worried about the payslip on the same day.
fieldNote: He **uses AI daily** to support practice rather than authorise site work, preserving the distinction between curiosity and electrical competence.
His **renewal risk** exists before major automation, so moderate savings and a useful tool do not make the mild scenario calm.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts and ask for written renewal standards and dates
Postpone buying the larger used car until written job renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try the tools and show us what they actually do to junior hours. I'd volunteer to test an AI note tool with my supervisor during paid time, but not to become the person signing off work I don't understand. I want to learn quickly without selling the boss a story about being ready when I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if faster planning lets the experienced people do more with fewer juniors. Anya's sewing is physical, but fewer costume orders could still hurt if customers use cheaper design and planning to cut their budgets; I don't know how that would work out. Two months saved doesn't give us room to treat both wages as guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for a four-week paid note-tool trial, with the supervisor checking every example from completed repairs. In the first year I'd offer two weekend furniture-assembly slots a month through the local noticeboard, taking bookings only within my ability and only if the fee covers travel. I'd agree the times with Anya first, because extra income isn't useful if it stops the household working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a temptation to say yes to everything. The useful part of having a plan is deciding which extra jobs not to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why furniture assembly rather than weekend wiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can assemble a flat-pack cupboard without pretending my certificate lets me run electrical jobs alone. I'd leave anything involving wiring to a qualified person and be honest about what the assembly fee includes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Anya have time to cover those weekends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd choose two slots together, with me taking another block of childcare in return. If the times don't fit, I won't book the work; I can't count family time as a free resource.

say: I'd test tools against **real junior hours** rather than just accept a claim of progress.
I'd volunteer for **supervised tool trials** without pretending I can sign off work I do not understand.
think: My **hours could shrink** if experienced electricians cover more work without junior help.
Anya's **physical sewing work** is not a guarantee of unchanged orders or a second wage that always covers us.
do: Request a **four-week paid trial** of AI repair notes with every example checked by the supervisor.
Offer **two monthly assembly slots** within my ability only where fees cover travel.
Agree **childcare and times** with Anya before taking furniture bookings.
feel: **Anxious and tempted** to accept too much, using the plan to set limits.
S1.quote: I can't count family time as a free resource.
fieldNote: The **side work** is furniture assembly rather than unsupervised electrical contracting, with travel costs, ability and childcare conditions explicit.
He recognises **household uncertainty** without claiming theatre sewing disappears on a date the card does not specify.

steps.text: Trial AI repair notes for four paid supervised weeks
Offer two monthly assembly slots only with suitable skills, travel fees and agreed childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots around 2031, but a junior cannot spend that gap just being hopeful. I'd ask the employer which tasks it will pay me to learn. I'd rather hear an awkward answer than tell my family I've secured a future because I tried a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big cut to my paid hours when robots can take the simpler fitting work around 2031, with possible cuts from planning earlier. The furniture jobs could face the same robots, so that is temporary extra money, not a permanent escape. With two children and a mortgage, I keep waking up to work out how quickly our two-month reserve would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd offer the two affordable furniture slots while there is demand, with Anya agreeing childcare, and put any money left after travel into the household reserve. I'd ask two nearby firms about advertised supervised service posts with paid practical training. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply only if the written wage after travel covers our bills, keeping the present job until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I keep making lists. The numbers still don't add up. I don't want to mistake staying busy for finding an answer that protects the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before changing employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guaranteed hours, who supervises me and whether the training time is paid. I'd compare the whole week after travel costs, not just the hourly rate at the top of an advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much furniture income are you assuming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None until someone books and pays, and only the amount left after travel would go into savings. If the jobs stop, we'd review the household budget rather than borrow to advertise a business nobody is using.

say: I'd ask for **paid learning tasks** rather than use the gap before robots as a reason to hope.
I'd explain **2028 thinking changes** and robots around 2031 without claiming an app secures my future.
think: I expect a **big hours cut** when robots take simpler fitting work around 2031, with possible earlier planning cuts.
Furniture assembly offers **temporary money**, not a permanent escape from robots or guaranteed mortgage protection.
do: Offer **two affordable assembly slots** with agreed childcare, saving only paid income left after travel.
Ask two firms about **advertised supervised service posts** with paid practical training.
Apply after 2028 only with **affordable written wages**, guaranteed hours and paid training before leaving this job.
feel: **Alarmed**, waking to calculate how quickly two months of savings could disappear.
S2.quote: I don't want to mistake staying busy for finding an answer that protects the mortgage.
fieldNote: His **expected loss** mainly follows physical robots around 2031, while thinking-work changes can create earlier pressure on junior hours.
He counts **no side income** before payment and requires signed affordable job terms, avoiding the idea that enthusiasm or activity guarantees security.

steps.text: Offer two monthly assembly slots only with demand, affordable travel and agreed childcare
Save only assembly income left after paid travel costs
Apply after 2028 for posted supervised jobs with paid training and wages covering bills after travel
Keep current job until an offer with guaranteed paid hours is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to test a training route properly, not just collect courses. I'd ask for small paid practical classes where someone watches me doing the task. I don't mind whether a firm, college or public programme arranges it if the paid time and actual place are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could still fall, but I have longer to move past the simple tasks before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I still need work rather than a story about retiring just in time. I like trying things, but none of the routes is a guaranteed shelter from the whole change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol this winter in a weekend practical-testing class only if its fee is at most one hundred and eighty and it uses supervised equipment. I've saved that amount separately for work learning, so I wouldn't take it from the two-month emergency reserve. In the first year after 2031 I'd use new planning tools on supervised jobs during paid time, and keep the two furniture slots only if demand and childcare still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with enough time to try something and check whether it helps. A small class is a risk I can price; promising myself a safe career is a risk I can't price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class is cancelled or the equipment is missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the refund terms before paying, and only enrol if I can recover the fee when the promised workshop doesn't run. A lesson about equipment needs actual equipment, not an apology and a slideshow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra class let you take electrical work on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still be a junior needing the right supervision and checks. I want a bit more competence, not a certificate to wave at somebody who assumes it means a licence I don't have.

say: I'd favour **tested practical routes** over collecting course names without useful paid work behind them.
I care about real places and **paid time**, whichever organisation arranges them.
think: My **income could fall**, but five years gives me longer to move beyond the simplest tasks before 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I need earned income without assuming any new skill is permanently protected.
do: Enrol in **supervised testing** within the separate 180 learning pot, preserving emergency savings and requiring suitable refunds.
Use **new planning tools** on supervised jobs during paid time after 2031.
Keep **two furniture slots** only if demand, affordable travel and agreed childcare still fit.
feel: **Anxious but willing**, able to price a small class without claiming a safe career is guaranteed.
S3.quote: A lesson about equipment needs actual equipment, not an apology and a slideshow.
fieldNote: The **course money** is separately saved, with a cap and refund condition rather than an unmentioned withdrawal from emergency savings.
He retains **junior supervision** after the class, so fast learning and another short certificate never authorise independent electrical practice.

steps.text: Enrol from separate 180 learning pot only with supervised equipment and suitable refunds
Use planning tools on paid supervised jobs after 2031
Keep two assembly slots only with demand, affordable travel and agreed childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets families prepare without naming one safe job for every child. I'd ask the school about work visits in several fields and let the children ask their own questions. I'd still want adult classes checked for actual equipment and useful tasks rather than sold with a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage and my next work renewal still worry me today, even if the big change waits until 2036. I'll be fifty-three at the thinking-AI date and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be sixteen and twenty-five in 2036, and I can't assume either their earnings or our mortgage balance then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same capped, refundable practical class now and keep the emergency reserve separate. This year I'd ask the school about free work visits across several fields for the children. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for advertised supervised service posts if my hours fall, comparing guaranteed pay and travel before leaving the current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next six months, but less pressed by the distant change. I can be curious with the children without acting as though the family needs a new future picked by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the older child about choosing studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what they enjoy and find an adult doing that work to talk with them. I wouldn't tell them to copy my trade or avoid every thinking subject because of a picture we discussed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A non-renewal notice or a repeated cut in paid hours would make me compare real vacancies straight away. Having ten years before AGI doesn't mean the employer has promised me ten years of wages.

say: I'd seek **varied work visits** so the children can ask questions rather than be assigned a supposedly safe career.
I'd want adult courses checked for **real equipment** and useful tasks instead of a forecast.
think: The **mortgage and renewal** already worry me, even with the major change a decade away.
I cannot budget around **future child earnings** or assume the mortgage is cleared when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Enrol in **supervised testing** within the separate 180 learning pot, preserving emergency savings and requiring suitable refunds.
Ask the school this year about **free work visits** across several fields.
Apply after hours fall for **advertised supervised posts**, checking guaranteed pay and travel before leaving the current job.
feel: **Anxious about near-term renewal**, but able to approach the distant future with curiosity.
S4.quote: Having ten years before AGI doesn't mean the employer has promised me ten years of wages.
fieldNote: His **renewal risk** remains relevant with distant technological change, supporting anxiety without importing an early AGI event.
He **advances the children's ages** correctly and avoids assuming their future income or a cleared mortgage will finance his later work transition.

steps.text: Enrol from separate 180 learning pot only with supervised equipment and suitable refunds
Ask the school about free work visits in several fields
Apply after hours fall for advertised supervised posts with affordable guaranteed pay after travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect simpler paid work to shrink before I've built enough skill to compete for different tasks. Real supervised training with clear fees, paid time and actual equipment would help. I'd want an employer to state the paid hours instead of treating my enthusiasm as a promise I can live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether learning quickly costs somebody else time at home. I can make another list every night, but Anya and the children still need me to do my share. Being keen doesn't give my family an extra pair of hands.

headlineQuote: Being keen doesn't give my family an extra pair of hands.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still requiring supervised tests after earlier hotel maintenance work.
He has **two months saved**, typical pay, some nearby firms, two schoolchildren and a mortgage with costume-sewing partner Anya.
He uses **AI daily** for checked practice and welcomes small risks, while job renewal already makes the mild picture anxious.
Rapid AGI makes him **alarmed about hours**; side work remains temporary and classes retain cost, equipment, refund and supervision conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink simpler paid work before he builds enough skill for different tasks.
whatWouldHelp: **Real supervised training** should specify fees, paid time and actual equipment.
Employers should state **paid hours** rather than assume enthusiasm funds a household.
